content: Clinical engineering is a specialized field that focuses on the application of engineering principles and technology to enhance and deliver healthcare services. While its origins can be traced back to the 1940s, the term clinical engineering was first introduced in 1969. Over time, the field has evolved from being primarily research-oriented to focusing on the maintenance of medical equipment. Efforts have been made to expand the scope of clinical engineering to include activities such as evaluating equipment before purchase, investigating incidents, managing equipment, improving productivity, ensuring cost-effectiveness, integrating information systems, and promoting patient safety. However, these efforts have achieved only limited success. The history of applying engineering to medicine can be traced back several centuries, depending on the perspective. The first modern professional meeting dedicated to the application of engineering in medicine likely occurred in 1948, as noted by the Alliance for Engineering in Medicine and Biology. The term clinical engineering was explicitly mentioned for the first time in a 1969 paper by Landoll and Caceres. Dr. Cesar A. Caceres, a cardiologist, is widely credited with coining the term. In the early 1970s, clinical engineering was anticipated to grow significantly, with estimates suggesting the need for 5,000 to 8,000 clinical engineers in the United States. This translated to approximately five to ten clinical engineers per 250,000 people or one clinical engineer per 250 hospital beds. However, at that time, only 300 to 400 clinical engineers were employed in hospitals. Over the following decades, there has been no evidence of significant growth in the number of clinical engineers, and there may even have been a decline. For example, the International Certification Commission for Clinical Engineers (ICC) was established in the early 1970s under the Association for the Advancement of Medical Instrumentation (AAMI) to provide formal certification for clinical engineers. Another certification program, the American Board of Clinical Engineering (ABCE), was created by academic institutions offering graduate degrees in clinical engineering. In 1979, the ABCE dissolved, and its certified members were integrated into the ICC certification program. By 1985, only 350 clinical engineers had been certified. In 1999, after extensive deliberation and a survey in 1998 that revealed insufficient demand for the certification program, AAMI decided to suspend the program and stopped accepting new applicants as of July 1999. A new certification program was launched in 2002 under the sponsorship of the American College of Clinical Engineering (ACCE) and administered by the ACCE Healthcare Technology Foundation. In 2004, the first year of the new certification process, 112 individuals were certified based on their previous ICC certification, and three new certifications were granted. By mid-2007, a total of 147 individuals had been certified under this program. A clinical engineer is defined as a professional who supports and advances patient care by applying engineering and managerial skills to healthcare technology. This role often involves collaboration with a wide range of professionals, including physicians, nurses, medical technologists, IT specialists, pharmacists, administrators, medical device manufacturers, and regulatory authorities. Clinical engineers typically work alongside Biomedical Equipment Technicians (BMETs) to maintain and support medical devices used in patient care settings. This definition was formally adopted by the ACCE Board of Directors on May 13, 1991. However, two issues remain unresolved in this definition. First, the distinction between clinical engineer and biomedical engineer is often unclear, as the terms are frequently used interchangeably. Some hospitals refer to their medical equipment maintenance departments as clinical engineering departments, while others use the term biomedical engineering departments. Technicians are almost universally referred to as biomedical equipment technicians (BMETs), regardless of the department's name. Generally, biomedical engineer is considered a broader term that includes engineers involved in designing medical devices for manufacturers, whereas clinical engineers typically work in hospitals, addressing issues related to the use of equipment in patient care settings. The second issue pertains to the educational background required for clinical engineers. Certification programs generally expect applicants to hold a bachelor's degree in engineering, although exceptions may be made for individuals with sufficient years of engineering practice. In general, clinical engineers are trained as engineers and possess the academic credentials to demonstrate their qualifications. The management of healthcare technology is becoming increasingly complex. The challenges and opportunities associated with this evolution were explored in the article The Future of Clinical Engineering, published in the IEEE EMBS magazine in 2003.
